content:
Apple has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, accusing the latter of stealing trade secrets. The case has been reassigned to U.S. District Judge Edward Davila, replacing the magistrate judge who was originally handling it. Details of the case are as follows.

Following the reassignment, the hearing originally scheduled for October has been cancelled.

In civil suits filed with the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, cases are randomly assigned to a district judge or a magistrate judge. If a case is assigned to a magistrate judge, all parties must indicate whether they consent to having the magistrate judge handle the case in its entirety.

This is because a district judge has the authority to preside over a federal civil case from start to finish, whereas a magistrate judge can only do so with the consent of all parties.

On the same day Apple filed its lawsuit against two former employees, OpenAI and Jony Ive's company io Products, accusing them of stealing trade secrets, the case was randomly assigned to Magistrate Judge Virginia K. DeMarchi.

This meant that all parties in the lawsuit had to submit a form indicating whether they agreed to having Judge DeMarchi handle the case in its entirety.

Apple appears to have rejected this arrangement. The company filed a "consent or declination" form yesterday (which has not yet been made public), and this form appears to have triggered the process of reassigning the case to a district judge.

In the absence of any other documents explaining the reassignment, there is widespread speculation that Apple has opted out of having a magistrate judge preside over the case.

The case has therefore been reassigned to U.S. District Judge Edward Davila, with Magistrate Judge Nathanael Cousins handling matters related to discovery.

Following the reassignment, the initial case management conference previously scheduled for October 13 before Judge DeMarchi has been cancelled and must be rescheduled before Judge Davila.

However, two other deadlines remain in effect: the parties must hold a settlement conference and discuss a discovery plan by September 22, and then submit preliminary disclosures and a joint case management statement by October 6.
